name: Treadmill desk

lead: A treadmill desk lets you walk slowly while you work. People use it to add low-intensity movement to the day, which supports a leaner physique over time, and some like the upright stance compared with sitting.

Slow walking raises energy expenditure above resting levels while you type or read. Trials report more daily activity and modest weight changes; effects on posture and appearance have not been studied.

paras: Users walk at an easy pace, typically under 2 mph, for part of the workday and alternate with sitting or standing. Weight and fitness changes build over weeks and months.

Studies report slight effects on pointing accuracy and number recall. Cardiometabolic benefit is not established. Safety keys stop the belt if you step off, and some people find fine mouse work harder while walking.

angle.text: Treadmill desks add low-intensity walking to the workday, which raises daily energy use and supports a gradual move toward a leaner physique. Trials show more movement and modest weight changes.

lead: A treadmill desk is a computer desk adapted so the user walks slowly on a treadmill while working. It is intended to reduce sitting time and raise energy expenditure above resting levels, rather than to deliver aerobic exercise.[1]

People use one to look leaner and fitter through a simple chain: slow walking through the workday adds calories burned on top of resting metabolism, adds up across weeks, and can nudge body fat and waist measurements downward while also keeping the user upright instead of slumped in a chair.[1][2][3] In lifting forums, desk treadmills are mentioned as a way to rack up steps and keep conditioning going alongside training.[4][5]

Wikipedia credits Nathan Edelson with proposing the idea in the late 1980s, and James Levine of the Mayo Clinic is credited as its popular inspiration.[1] A 2021 meta-analysis of 13 studies with 351 participants found that treadmill desks raised energy expenditure by about 105 kcal per hour in laboratory studies and trimmed sitting time modestly in workplace studies.[6]

The research base is larger than for most appearance-adjacent gear: it includes a one-year prospective trial, several randomised workplace trials, a 2023 twelve-month cluster trial and a series of systematic reviews, covering activity, body weight, cardiometabolic markers, cognition and productivity.[6][7][8][9]
infobox: About 100 to 130 kcal per hour above sitting (Mayo Clinic estimate) [1]

paras: Treadmill desks fall into three categories: desks designed to cover a traditional treadmill, treadmills designed to fit under a standing desk, and integrated units made by the original manufacturer.[1] Wikipedia reports a recommended walking speed of under 2 miles per hour so that typing and reading remain practical.[1]

Users who tested treadmill desks reported that reading email and browsing were easier to manage than typing or writing while walking, and that phone calls could be disrupted by changes in breathing or by treadmill noise.[1] Ergonomic guidance matches that for any desk: wrists flat at the keyboard, elbows near 90 degrees, and eyes forward to the monitor.[1]

sections.h: How it is used to change appearance
paras: The appearance case rests on energy balance. Wikipedia cites Mayo Clinic estimates of about 100 to 130 kcal per hour above sitting at speeds under 2 mph, so several hours of walking-and-working per day add a few hundred kilocalories of expenditure without a separate gym session.[1] Researchers who have reviewed the field describe this as a way to lower sedentary time and increase energy expenditure in people with overweight or obesity.[2]

Practitioners describe the desk as a base layer under conventional training: steps and low-intensity movement accumulate during the working day, while lifting and cardio happen separately. Posts on a strength-training forum mention a desk treadmill as a convenient way to reach a daily step target and to keep walking while logging weight loss.[4][5] Because the pace is slow, the approach is typically described as incremental rather than as a quick change in body shape.

Edelson published articles in 1988 and 1989 and received a patent in 1993 for a portable version. Seth Roberts built one in 1996, and Levine popularised the concept after constructing one by placing a hospital tray over a treadmill as part of his work on non-exercise activity thermogenesis.[1] Roger Highfield, after testing one under Levine's supervision in 2006, helped spread the idea in the UK.[1]

TrekDesk, the first height-adjustable desk made to fit existing treadmills, appeared in 2009.[1] In 2013 novelist Amanda Filipacchi wrote a Wall Street Journal essay about buying treadmill desks, and in 2018 Abu Dhabi's health department launched a 10,000-steps-a-day challenge using treadmill desks.[1]

Consumer Reports published a July 2013 article of tips for using a desk treadmill and a November 2013 test of units priced between $750 and $1,500, recommending models with safety and personalisation features. A New York Times piece in 2015 titled 'The Downside of Treadmill Desks' examined limitations of the approach. Both are described in Wikipedia's account.[1]

Treadmill desks include a clip-on key that stops the belt when pulled and many pause automatically when the user steps off for more than about 20 seconds.[1] Participants advised keeping a conventional desk and alternating between sitting and walking while getting used to the setup.[1]

A study of implementation and adherence in a workplace treadmill desk intervention examined barriers users reported.[10] Qualitative work on people using treadmill desks when working from home reported experiences described as a 'game changer' by some participants.[11]

A 2021 meta-analysis found laboratory energy expenditure rose by 105.23 kcal per hour (95% CI 90.41 to 120.4) and workplace sitting fell by 1.73 minutes per hour; no significant blood pressure differences were found and the authors noted further studies are needed on cardiometabolic outcomes.[6] A separate meta-analysis of sedentary-reduction interventions in overweight and obesity found that those with an active component, such as a treadmill desk, reduced sedentary time, while interventions without one did not show the same effect.[12]

A 3-month randomised trial of 41 overweight or obese office workers compared a shared treadmill desk with usual working. Per the published abstract, the treadmill group took about 1,622 more steps per day and cut sedentary time by about 3.6 minutes per hour during working hours.[8]

A 2019 systematic review of active workstations in people with overweight or obesity found decreased sedentary time and increased energy expenditure, and the treadmill desk was the only workstation type for which body-weight management outcomes such as body fat percentage, body weight and waist and hip circumference were reported.[2] A 2015 review of standing and treadmill desks concluded that treadmill desks produced the greatest improvements in physiological outcomes, including postprandial glucose, HDL cholesterol and anthropometrics, while the authors noted the evidence was still limited.[13]

A 2007 Mayo Clinic analysis of office workers with obesity estimated that replacing sitting with walking-and-working for two to three hours a day could produce substantial weight loss over a year. Levine's team's actual 12-month trial in 2013, in 36 employees, reported mean weight loss of 1.4 kg, or 2.3 kg among obese participants.[1][7]

An acute randomised trial reported that replacing prolonged sitting with treadmill desk walking improved cardiometabolic risk markers in men and women.[14] Reviewers of the wider literature note that longer-term cardiometabolic outcomes remain an open question.[6]

Studies tested cognitive tasks while walking slowly. One examined Stroop, flanker and reading comprehension in 66 participants.[15] Another reported that slow walking did not negatively affect executive abilities.[16] A PLOS ONE study of 75 participants randomised to walk at 1.5 mph or sit reported a modest negative effect on number-sequence recall, and Levine reported lower mouse accuracy, per Wikipedia.[17][1] Wikipedia's summary of Levine's study gives a 14 percent drop in pointing speed and a 106 percent rise in mouse error rate, with typing less affected.[1]

A study examined transcriptionists' productivity.[18] A systematic review of active workstations covered productivity and performance outcomes and reported that treadmill and cycling workstations showed potential decreases in some single-session studies, while longer studies of 12 to 52 weeks reported no significant effect on productivity.[19] A study comparing sitting, standing and treadmill desks looked at psychobiological indicators of productivity.[20]

A 12-month cluster randomised trial of 66 overweight or obese office workers compared seated desks, sit-to-stand desks and treadmill desks, measuring behaviour with thigh-worn accelerometers. Treadmill users stood for longer bouts and took longer stepping bouts at 3 months, but at 12 months their typical sedentary bouts were about 9 minutes longer across the day than controls', and the authors concluded that sit-to-stand desks produced more favourable behaviour patterns than treadmill desks.[9]

A separate cluster randomised trial examined an active-workstation intervention's effect on daily waking physical behaviours.[21] In the workplace trial that tested implementation, researchers documented adherence issues.[10] The overall pattern in reviews is that use of treadmill desks tends to be partial: people alternate walking and sitting.[1][6]

A 1-year prospective trial of 36 employees tested whether treadmill desks would raise daily activity and cut sedentary time.[7] A 3-month randomised trial randomised 41 overweight or obese office workers to a shared treadmill desk or usual working.[8] A 24-week randomised crossover trial of 20 overweight and obese physicians examined treadmill desk use together with exercise counselling.[22] A cluster randomised trial examined active workstations and daily waking physical behaviours,[21] with a follow-up on sit-to-stand and treadmill desks among overweight and obese seated office workers.[9] An acute randomised trial found that reducing prolonged sitting with a treadmill desk improved cardiometabolic risk markers in men and women.[14] Systematic reviews of standing and treadmill desks and of active workstations have assessed health and performance outcomes.[13][3] Wikipedia also notes a 2018 Cochrane review that found it unclear whether treadmill desks effectively reduce sitting.[1]

Treadmill desks are one of several active workstations, alongside sit-to-stand desks and cycling desks, which the same reviews group together.[3][19] Walking pads, under-desk treadmills and step-count targets are the same idea in different forms, and strength-training forum members commonly pair them with lifting and a diet plan.[4][5]

lore.intro: Treadmill desks appear on strength-training forums mostly as a step-count tool for people who sit for work.[4][5]
